statement: Genesis 6–9 shares a clustered flood-story sequence with earlier Mesopotamian traditions: divine decision to destroy humanity, warning of a favored survivor, construction of a vessel, preservation of life, survival of the deluge, post-flood sacrifice, and a divine response after the sacrifice.

sources.author: Genesis
sources.access_note: Used for the observable sequence in the biblical narrative.

sources.citation: John Day, “Comparative Ancient Near Eastern Study: The Genesis Flood Narrative in Relation to Ancient Near Eastern Flood Accounts,” in Biblical Interpretation and Method (Oxford University Press, 2013), pp. 74–88.
sources.author: John Day
sources.access_note: Oxford abstract explicitly compares Genesis with the Sumerian, Atraḫasīs, Gilgamesh, and Berossus flood traditions and weighs parallels rather than merely counting them.

does_not_demonstrate: Shared narrative structure does not by itself identify a single Mesopotamian source text.
The comparison does not prove the Genesis authors had direct access to a surviving Atraḫasīs or Gilgamesh manuscript.
notes: Observation claim supporting the separate transmission interpretation.
